title: University of Winnipeg - UWinnipeg-Yale-MIT collaboration provides an origin story of black hole dark matter

content:
For more than a century, black holes have captured our imagination. Predicted by Einstein's theory of general relativity, they have now moved from theory to observation.


Dr. Evan McDonough

A team of physicists, including collaborators from UWinnipeg, has published a new paper showing that new subatomic particles at high energies can underpin the black hole explanation for dark matter. The Winnipeg-Toronto-Yale-MIT collaboration shows that new particles at high energies give a dramatic boost to the formation of black holes in the very early universe, providing an origin story for black hole dark matter.

The University of Winnipeg has a strong record of undergraduates publishing in top physics journals.

Dr. Evan McDonough


Dario Lorenzoni

"It's pushing the boundaries of what we know, and what we understand," explains the lead author of the paper, Dario Lorenzoni, a PhD student at UManitoba and supervised by UWinnipeg's Dr. Evan McDonough, who is also a contributor to this paper.

Black holes may also help solve one of cosmology's biggest puzzles. Roughly 85% of the matter in the universe is invisible, detectable only through its gravity, which holds galaxies together.

This "dark matter" could be made of black holes that formed not from collapsing stars, but in the first moments after the Big Bang. These are known as primordial black holes.

"Primordial black holes provide an easy answer for dark matter," says Dr. McDonough, "but the mystery becomes their origin: What happened in the first moments of the universe to bring these black holes into being? Our work provides an answer to this question."

Co-authors on the paper include Dr. McDonough's Indigenous Summer Scholar Kyle Weittmeier ; and Zachary Ireland, also an undergraduate student who came to UWinnipeg in summer 2025 from the University of Toronto to work with Dr. McDonough.

Also on the team is Dr. Sarah Geller, an NSF Fellow at Yale University who was at UWinnipeg in 2024 , and Dr. David Kaiser, a renowned physicist and historian at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

"The University of Winnipeg has a strong record of undergraduates publishing in top physics journals" adds Dr. McDonough. "This is one of the benefits of being at a small school that is so full of opportunities."

Dr. Evan McDonough is an Associate Professor at the University of Winnipeg and the Director of the Winnipeg Institute for Theoretical Physics. The WITP is the largest center for theoretical physics in Canada aside from the Perimeter Institute. With help from the Perimeter and Quantum Horizons Alberta, the WITP is spearheading a theoretical physics boom on the prairies.
